summary: This document describes and discusses the textual encodings of PKIX, PKCS, and CMS structures. These encodings, with their BEGIN and END lines, are well known and widely implemented, and this document records how they work.

eli5.summary: Keys and certificates are binary data, which does not paste well into emails. This describes the common way of turning them into plain text with a header and footer line.

subtitle: The BEGIN/END, base64 text format for certificates, keys and requests, written down so every tool agrees.

tldr.problem: Certificates, keys and similar structures are binary, which does not travel well in email or text documents. Many libraries had their own slightly different text format, similar to but not identical with PEM.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a textual encoding: a line of five hyphens, BEGIN and a label, base64 data wrapped at 64 characters, and a matching END line, with a fixed label for each structure type.
tldr.outcome: It records the de facto rules and adds recommendations so that future implementations interoperate. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Line length
facts.value: 64 base64 characters, except the last line

today: RFC 7468 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Text Encoding
sections.content:
Many security standards define ASN.1 data that is normally sent in the binary BER or DER encodings. A binary format cannot be passed through text channels such as email or text documents. A text form is also easy to edit: a user can join several certificates into a chain by copy and paste.

The tradition goes back to Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM, RFC 1421), which was based on RFC 934. Today the format is sometimes called "PEM encoding". Variants include OpenPGP ASCII armor and the OpenSSH key file format. The RFC says many PKIX, PKCS and CMS libraries implement something similar to, but not identical with, PEM.

This document specifies the textual encoding, articulates the de facto rules most implementations follow, and gives recommendations and common names for the syntax elements. It covers certificates, CRLs, public keys, PKCS #10 requests, PKCS #7, CMS, PKCS #8 private keys and attribute certificates.
sections.eli5: Computers like bytes, but people and email like letters. This turns the bytes into letters so you can paste a key into a message.

sections.title: The General Format
sections.content:
An encoding starts with a line made of -----BEGIN , a label and -----, and ends with -----END , the same label and -----. Between these "encapsulation boundaries" is base64 data as defined in Section 4 of RFC 4648. There are exactly five hyphen-minus characters on both ends and exactly one space between BEGIN or END and the label.

Generators MUST wrap the base64 so each line has exactly 64 characters, except the final line, and MUST NOT emit extra whitespace. Parsers MAY accept other line sizes. Generators MUST use the same label on the END line as on the BEGIN line, though parsers MAY ignore a mismatch. Labels are case-sensitive and uppercase.

Text before the boundaries is allowed and parsers MUST NOT malfunction on it. Parsers SHOULD ignore whitespace and other non-base64 characters and MUST handle different newline conventions. A file MAY hold several encoded items, such as several certificates. Unlike legacy PEM, OpenPGP armor and OpenSSH, this format does not define headers alongside the data.
sections.eli5: It is like a package with a label on top and the same label on the bottom. Inside, the contents are written in a plain alphabet, 64 letters to a line.

sections.title: Strict, Standard and Lax Grammars
sections.content:
The RFC gives ABNF grammars (RFC 5234) at three levels of tolerance. The standard grammar allows blanks at ends of lines and several newline styles. The lax grammar accepts any mixture of whitespace outside the boundaries and is not line oriented at all; the RFC warns that this risks accepting text, such as a sample snippet, that was never meant to be accepted.

The strict grammar requires full lines of exactly 64 base64 characters followed by a final line of up to 15 groups of 4 characters, and an end-of-line after each boundary. New implementations SHOULD emit the strict format. The choice of parsing strategy depends on the context.

The RFC notes that most existing parsers ignore blanks at line ends, while blanks at the start of lines or inside the base64 are far less compatible.
sections.eli5: There are three sets of rules: a very picky one for writing, and two more relaxed ones for reading messy input. When writing, be picky.

sections.title: The Labels and What They Hold
sections.content:
Each label implies a particular ASN.1 structure. The encoded data MUST be BER, with DER preferred or strongly preferred depending on the type. For example, CERTIFICATE holds a PKIX Certificate from RFC 5280, X509 CRL a CertificateList, and CERTIFICATE REQUEST a PKCS #10 CertificationRequest (RFC 2986).

PRIVATE KEY holds an unencrypted PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo (RFC 5208), which RFC 5958 renamed OneAsymmetricKey; the two are semantically identical and can be told apart by version number. ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY holds an EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE an AttributeCertificate (RFC 5755), and PUBLIC KEY a SubjectPublicKeyInfo.

For PKCS #7 (PKCS7, RFC 2315) and CMS (CMS, RFC 5652) the structure is ContentInfo. PKCS #7 is old and superseded by CMS, so implementations SHOULD NOT generate PKCS #7 when CMS is an alternative.

For certificates, tools often emit explanatory text before the BEGIN and after the END lines. If so, it SHOULD relate to the certificate. The file extension .crt SHOULD be used for the textual encoding of a certificate, although many tools still use .cer.
sections.eli5: The top line tells you what is in the package: a certificate, a public key, a request, and so on. The label decides how to read the letters inside.

sections.title: Legacy Label Variants
sections.content:
Some older or less common labels exist in the wild. The RFC standardizes one label for each type and says what to do with the variants. Generators MUST emit CERTIFICATE and MUST NOT emit X509 CERTIFICATE or X.509 CERTIFICATE. They MUST emit X509 CRL and MUST NOT emit CRL. They MUST emit CERTIFICATE REQUEST, though parsers MAY treat NEW CERTIFICATE REQUEST as equivalent.

The label CERTIFICATE CHAIN has been used for a degenerate PKCS #7 structure holding only certificates. Generators MUST NOT generate it, and parsers SHOULD NOT treat it as equivalent to PKCS7. Appendix A supplies examples of these non-conforming labels for interoperability testing.
sections.eli5: Over the years people wrote the top line in different ways. The rule now is to write it one way, but understand a few of the old ways if you must.

sections.title: Why DER Is Preferred
sections.content: Appendix B, which is informative, explains the DER preference. DER is a restricted profile of BER, so every DER encoding is also BER, but only one BER encoding of a value is the DER one. It matters because a digital signature is supposed to be computed over the DER encoding, cryptographic hashes used for identification are in practice computed over DER, and DER always states lengths up front, so a parser can predict memory use.
sections.eli5: BER is like many ways to write down the same number; DER picks exactly one. When everyone writes it the same way, checking signatures works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Data in this format often comes from untrusted sources, so parsers must handle unexpected data without causing security vulnerabilities. The RFC defines no canonical encoding. Allowing text instead of binary is one ambiguity; treating several labels as similar, and variations in whitespace or non-base64 characters, add more. These ambiguities can also create opportunities for side channels.

Anyone who needs a canonical form or wants to fingerprint an object must decode the structure and re-encode it as DER.
sections.eli5: The same message can be written with different spaces and labels, so do not compare the raw text. Turn it back into bytes first.

viz.caption: SHAPE OF A TEXTUAL ENCODING (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC)

data.title: Encapsulation boundaries
data.code:
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
<base64 data, 64 characters per line>
<final line, 64 characters or fewer>
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
